summary: This informational RFC defines a data format for shared brotli compression, adding shared dictionaries, large window support, and a container format to brotli (RFC 7932). These give significant compression gains.

plainLanguage.summary: Shared brotli is the brotli compression format with three additions. A dictionary can be agreed in advance and used by both sides, so the encoder can point at text the decoder already has. The window can be made much larger, so a match far back in a big file can still be used. And there is a container format that can hold several files and refer to dictionaries. Everything stays compatible with ordinary brotli.

questions: how does a brotli shared dictionary work
what is the shared brotli framing format
subtitle: Brotli compression extended with shared dictionaries, a huge sliding window and a container format.

tldr.problem: Regular brotli compresses each stream on its own, so it cannot use data that the sender and receiver already share, and its back references are limited to a 24-bit distance.
tldr.mechanism: Shared brotli adds shared dictionaries in two forms, LZ77 dictionaries and custom static dictionaries, a large window mode with window bits from 10 to 62, and a framing format that stores several resources and refers to dictionaries.
tldr.outcome: The formats give significant compression gains over regular brotli and stay backwards compatible with it, so a decoder that does not know about the extensions can still read an ordinary brotli stream.

today: RFC 9841 is an Informational document published in September 2025. It updates RFC 7932 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated, and it is the authoritative specification of the shared brotli formats.

sections.title: What Shared Brotli Adds
sections.content:
The purpose of this specification is to extend the brotli compressed data format with new abilities that allow further compression gains. Shared dictionaries allow a static shared context between encoder and decoder for significant compression gains. Large window brotli allows much larger back reference distances, to give compression gains for files over 16 MiB. The framing format is a container format that allows storage of multiple resources and references to dictionaries.

The document is the authoritative specification of the shared brotli data formats and of the backwards compatible changes to brotli. It defines the data format of serialized shared dictionaries, the data format of the framing format, the encoding of window bits and distances for large window brotli in the brotli data format, and the encoding of shared dictionary references in the brotli data format.

The scope is a data format for shared brotli compression, adding support for dictionaries and extended features to brotli. The text assumes a basic background in programming at the level of bits and other primitive data representations; familiarity with LZ77 coding is helpful but not required. Compliance is defined in the usual way: a compliant decompressor must be able to accept and decompress any data set that conforms to the specification, and a compliant compressor must produce data sets that conform to it.
sections.plainLanguage: Compression works by saying "copy this from a bit earlier". Two things limit how well that works. The sender and receiver can only refer to text one of them has already sent, and only within a limited distance. Shared brotli loosens both limits, and adds a container format so several files can travel together with their dictionary.

sections.title: Shared Dictionaries
sections.content:
A shared dictionary is a piece of data shared by a compressor and a decompressor. The compressor can take advantage of the dictionary context to encode the input in a more compact manner, and the compressor and decompressor must use exactly the same dictionary. A shared dictionary is specially useful to compress short input sequences.

There are two methods of sharing context. An LZ77 dictionary lets the encoder and decoder refer to a given sequence of bytes, and multiple LZ77 dictionaries can be set. A custom static dictionary is a word list with transforms: the encoder and decoder replace the static dictionary data with the data in the shared dictionary. The original static dictionary is described in RFC 7932, and the original data from its appendices is replaced. It is also possible to switch this dictionary dynamically based on the data compression context, or to include a reference to the original dictionary in the custom dictionary.

If no shared dictionary is set, the decoder behaves the same as in RFC 7932 on a brotli stream. If one is set, it can set LZ77 dictionaries, override static dictionary words, and override transforms.

With a custom word list set, three decoder behaviours are overridden: the static dictionary data is replaced by one or more word lists from the custom static dictionary; the size bits at the end of the appendix are replaced by a custom value per word list; and the copy length for a static dictionary reference must be between 4 and 31 and may not be a length for which the size bits of that dictionary are zero. With a custom transforms list set and no context dependency, the list of word transformations is overridden by custom prefixes, suffixes and operations, and the transform identifier must be smaller than the number of transforms in the custom list.

A context-dependent dictionary includes a lookup table of 64 word list and transform list combinations. When resolving a static dictionary word, the decoder computes the literal context ID as in RFC 7932 and uses it as the index into the lookup tables to select the word list and transforms. If the dictionary is not context dependent, that ID is implicitly zero. If a distance goes beyond the dictionary for the current ID and several combinations are defined, the next dictionary is used: with a context-dependent dictionary, the index matching the current context comes first and then the order defined in the shared dictionary; otherwise the defined order is used as it is.

The transform operations are identified by numerical IDs. Operations 0 to 20 are the ones specified in RFC 7932, and two more are added here: ShiftFirst and ShiftAll, which transform specifically encoded scalars. A SCALAR is a 7-, 11-, 16- or 21-bit unsigned integer encoded in one, two, three or four bytes, whose bits come from a pattern where the trailing bits may hold any value. ShiftAll starts at the beginning of the word and applies the transformation repeatedly until the whole word is transformed; ShiftFirst applies the same transformation but does not iterate.
sections.plainLanguage: A dictionary has two shapes. One is a block of bytes the encoder can point into as if it were the recent past, which is useful for short inputs where there is not enough history yet. The other replaces the built-in list of common words with a list of your own, optionally chosen per context, so the encoder can say "word 17 of list 3" and both sides know which word that is.

sections.title: Varints and the Dictionary Stream
sections.content:
A varint is encoded in base 128 in one or more bytes. The trailing bits of each byte carry the value, and the last byte must have its most significant bit clear while all other bytes must have it set to show there is a next byte. The maximum number of bits to read is 63; if a ninth byte is present with its most significant bit set, the stream is invalid.

The shared dictionary stream encodes a custom dictionary for brotli, including custom words and transforms. It may appear standalone or as the contents of a resource in a framing format container, and its format is fixed. It begins with a two-byte file signature, the bytes 91 and 0. Then comes a varint giving the LZ77 dictionary length, the number of bytes in the LZ77 dictionary or zero if there is none, whose maximum allowed value is the maximum possible sliding window size of brotli or large window brotli. The dictionary contents follow, then one byte giving the number of custom word lists, which may be 0 to 64.

Each word list starts with 28 bytes of size information, one unsigned 8-bit integer per word length from 4 to 31, where the value is the base-2 logarithm of the number of words of that length and zero means no words of that length; the maximum allowed length value is 15 bits. The offsets are computed from this, and the word data follows, with all the words of the shortest length first and then the next length, where for each length there are either zero or a positive power of two number of words.

Next comes one byte giving the number of custom transform lists, which may be 0 to 64. Each transform list starts with two bytes giving the length of the prefix and suffix data, which must be at least 1 because the list always ends with a zero-length stringlet even if it is empty. The stringlets follow: each has one byte of length, zero for the last entry of the list and 1 to 255 otherwise, with the terminating zero entry required to be present and to be the last byte of the prefix and suffix data, or the stream is rejected as invalid. Then one byte gives the number of transformation triplets, and each triplet has one byte indexing the prefix, one byte indexing the suffix and one byte giving the operation index. If and only if at least one transform uses ShiftFirst or ShiftAll, a further two bytes of parameters follow per transform, which must be zero for other operations and are read as an unsigned 16-bit integer by the two shift operations.

If there is more than one custom word list or more than one custom transform list, one byte gives the number of dictionaries, from 1 to 64, each a combination of a word list and a transform list; the next dictionary is used when the distance goes beyond the previous one, and with a context map the dictionary matching the context moves to the front for that context. A dictionary map follows, with one byte indexing a custom word list or the value that means the built-in default word list, one byte indexing a custom transform list or the value that means the built-in default transform list, and one byte saying whether a context map is present. When it is, 64 bytes give, for each of the 64 literal contexts, the index into the dictionary map of the first dictionary to use for that context.
sections.plainLanguage: The dictionary itself is a file with a fixed layout: a signature, the block of raw bytes that acts as an LZ77 dictionary, the word lists with a small table saying how many words of each length, and the transform lists with their prefixes and suffixes. Everything that is a count is written in a variable-length form where each byte says whether another byte follows.

sections.title: Large Window and Shared Brotli Streams
sections.content:
Large window brotli allows a sliding window beyond the 24-bit maximum of regular brotli. The compressed data stream is backwards compatible with brotli and may differ in two ways. In the encoding of the window size in the stream header, a new pattern of 14 bits is supported: eight bits with the value 00010001 to indicate a large window brotli stream, followed by six bits of window size that must be in the range 10 to 62.

The second difference is the distance alphabet. In a large window brotli stream the maximum number of extra bits is 62, and the theoretical maximum size of the distance alphabet is 16 plus the number of direct distances plus 124 shifted left by the number of postfix bits. This overrides the value given for the distance alphabet size in RFC 7932 and affects the number of bits in the encoding of the simple prefix code for distances. An additional limitation applies despite the large allowed alphabet size: the alphabet may not contain a distance symbol able to represent a distance larger than (1 shifted left by 63) minus 4 when its extra bits have their maximum value, which depends on the number of postfix bits and direct distances. A decoder that does not support 64-bit integers may reject a stream if the window size is higher than 30, or if a distance symbol can encode a distance larger than 2147483644.

A shared brotli compressed data stream without a framing format is backwards compatible with brotli, with three optional differences: LZ77 dictionaries are supported, custom static dictionaries that replace or extend the static dictionary of RFC 7932 with different words or transforms are supported, and the stream may have the format of regular brotli or the format of large window brotli.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary brotli can only look back about 16 MiB, because the distance field is 24 bits wide. The large window mode reuses a spare pattern in the stream header to say that the window can be up to 62 bits wide, with the distances stored in a larger alphabet. The bits that do this are new, so a decoder that does not understand them sees an invalid brotli stream and refuses it, which is what keeps the extension safe.

sections.title: The Framing Format
sections.content:
The framing format is a container that can hold several resources and refer to dictionaries. It begins with a four-byte file signature, the bytes 0x91, 0x0a, 0x42 and 0x52, where the first byte contains the invalid window-size combination for both brotli and large window brotli. Then comes one byte of container flags: bits 0 and 1 are a version indicator that must be zero, or the decoder must reject the stream as invalid, and bit 2 says whether the file contains a final footer, may contain metadata chunks and a central directory and may encode several resources, or whether it contains no final footer, no metadata chunks, no central directory and only a single resource. A sequence of chunks follows.

Each chunk starts with a varint giving its length, excluding the varint but including the header bytes and data that follow; a length of zero means the chunk type byte is not present and the type is assumed to be zero. Then one byte gives the chunk type: 0 padding, 1 metadata, 2 data, 3 first partial data, 4 middle partial data, 5 last partial data, 6 footer metadata, 7 global metadata, 8 repeat metadata, 9 central directory, 10 final footer.

Unless the chunk is a padding chunk, a central directory or a final footer, one byte gives the codec: 0 uncompressed, 1 keep decoder, 2 brotli, 3 shared brotli. If the codec is not uncompressed, a varint gives the uncompressed size in bytes of the data in the compressed stream. If the codec is shared brotli, one byte gives the number of dictionary references, and multiple references are possible under restrictions: there can be 1 serialized dictionary and 15 prefix dictionaries at most, and circular references are not allowed, meaning no dictionary reference may directly or indirectly use the chunk itself as its dictionary.

Each dictionary reference carries a byte of flags. Bits 0 and 1 give the source: an internal reference to a full resource by pointer, which may span one or more chunks and must point to a full data chunk or a first partial data chunk; an internal reference to the contents of a single chunk by pointer, which may point to any chunk with content, where a partial data chunk contributes only that part and the dictionary type may not be a serialized dictionary; or a reference by hash code of a resource, which may come from an external source such as a different container, and the user of the decoder must be able to provide the dictionary contents given its hash code or treat it as an error. Bits 2 and 3 give the type: a prefix dictionary, set in front of the sliding window, or a serialized dictionary in the shared brotli format. Bits 4 to 7 must be zero. For a hash-based reference there is one byte giving the type of hash, where the only supported value is 3, indicating a 256-bit HighwayHash, and 32 bytes of checksum. For a pointer-based reference there is a varint-encoded pointer to a chunk in the container, and that chunk must come earlier than the current chunk.

The chunk content then follows. For the uncompressed codec it is the raw bytes. For the keep decoder codec it is the continuation of the compressed stream that was interrupted at the end of the previous chunk, and the decoder from the previous chunk must be used with its state kept. Metadata chunks use a field format of a two-byte code, a varint length and that many bytes of content. The code must be two lowercase or two uppercase ASCII letters; a lowercase code the decoder does not recognise for the current chunk type, non-ASCII characters or non-alphabetic characters make the decoder reject the stream as invalid, while uppercase codes may be used for custom user metadata and can be ignored by a compliant decoder. Two field types are recognised for the metadata chunk: an id field carrying a name in UTF-8 that may be used as a filename, and an mt field carrying the modification type as microseconds since the epoch in a little-endian signed 64-bit integer.
sections.plainLanguage: The container is a sequence of chunks. Each chunk says how long it is, what kind it is, and how its data is compressed. The kinds cover the data itself, pieces of a resource that is too big for one chunk, and metadata about the resource. A chunk can also point at an earlier chunk and say "use that as the dictionary", either by position or by a checksum, which lets one file inside the container act as the dictionary for another.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations for brotli apply to shared brotli as well, and the same considerations apply to decoding the new file format streams, including shared dictionaries, the framing format and the shared brotli format. The dictionary must be treated with the same security precautions as the content, because a change to the dictionary can result in a change to the decompressed content.

The CRIME attack shows that it is a bad idea to compress data from mixed sources, public and private alike, and the data sources include not only the compressed data but also the dictionaries. Compressing secret cookies with a public-data-only dictionary still leaks information about the cookies. The dictionary can reveal information about the compressed data and the other way round: data compressed with the dictionary can reveal the contents of the dictionary when an adversary can control parts of the data and see the compressed size, and an adversary who controls the dictionary can learn about the compressed data.

The most robust defence against CRIME is not to compress private data, such as sensitive headers like cookies or content with personally identifiable information; the challenge has been to identify secrets within a large amount of data to be compressed, and one approach is a regular expression, another is to extend web template systems to let developers mark secrets that must not be compressed. A less robust but easier to implement defence is to randomize the compression algorithm, by adding randomly generated padding or varying the compression ratio, with the tricky part being to balance cost against security, since too much padding costs bandwidth and too little can be detected by traffic analysis. Another defence is not to use dictionaries for cross-domain requests, and to use shared brotli for the response only when the origin is the same as where the content is hosted, which prevents an adversary using a private dictionary with user secrets to compress content hosted on the adversary's origin.

The content of the dictionary itself should not be affected by external users, since allowing adversaries to control the dictionary allows a form of chosen plaintext attack. Instead, base the dictionary on content you control or on generic large-scale content such as a spoken language, and update it with large time intervals, days rather than seconds, to prevent fast probing. The use of HighwayHash for dictionary identifiers does not guarantee against collisions in an adversarial environment.
sections.plainLanguage: The dictionary is part of what gets compressed, so it leaks like the content does. If secret data is compressed together with anything the attacker can influence, the attacker can measure the output size and work out the secret. The safest rule is not to compress secrets at all; using a dictionary for one origin's own traffic is fine, but sharing it across origins is not.

items.title: Identity (0)
items.text: The word is used exactly as it appears in the dictionary.

items.title: OmitLast1 to OmitLast9 (1 to 9)
items.text: The last one to nine bytes of the word are dropped.

items.title: FermentFirst and FermentAll (10 and 11)
items.text: The first or all of the characters of the word are transformed.

items.title: OmitFirst1 to OmitFirst9 (12 to 20)
items.text: The first one to nine bytes of the word are dropped.

items.title: ShiftFirst and ShiftAll (21 and 22)
items.text: New in this document: they shift specifically encoded scalars in the word, and ShiftAll repeats until the whole word is transformed.

viz.caption: THE CHUNK TYPES IN THE FRAMING FORMAT

items.label: Padding chunk
items.desc: All bytes zero apart from the length varint.

items.label: Metadata chunk
items.desc: Metadata applying to the resource that starts in the next data chunk.

items.label: Data chunk
items.desc: The actual data of a resource.

items.label: First partial data chunk
items.desc: The first part of a resource split across several chunks.

items.label: Middle partial data chunk
items.desc: A part of a resource that is neither the first nor the last.

items.label: Last partial data chunk
items.desc: The final part of a resource split across several chunks.

items.label: Footer metadata chunk
items.desc: Metadata carried at the end of the container.

items.label: Global metadata chunk
items.desc: Metadata that applies to the whole container.

items.label: Central directory chunk
items.desc: Lists the resources in the container.

items.label: Final footer chunk
items.desc: The last chunk of the container.
